newsitem.title: IRAQ: FEATURE-Secretive sect survives on Tigris river in Baghdad.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Secretive sect survives on Tigris river in Baghdad.

text.p: Three brides standing knee-deep in a freezing pond shivered as a barefoot priest wielding a long stick splashed icy water on their faces, hands and chests.
"I stretch out my hands to the Lord, and praise the Only One," the priest in a spotless white robe murmured in Mandaean, an offshoot of Aramaic, the language of Jesus and his apostles.
It was part of a three-hour prayer that the priest, Khalaf Abidrabbah, 57, and his colleague Sattar Jabbar, 41, intoned as part of the marriage ritual.
The two exchanged roles as they sat, stood, sprinkled water over their hands, foreheads and arms and walked around mud pots full of charcoal and frankincense.

Each had a branch of myrtle in his white turban. Jabbar put a ring, also of myrtle, on the ring finger of each of the brides, who were all dressed in white. Later they were joined in the pond by the bridegrooms.

After the frankincense, readings from holy books, sprinkling with water and circling by the priests came the blood offering: Jabbar slaughtered three white ducks, one for each couple, and let their blood drip into the pond.
Iraq's secretive sect, the Sabaeans, has changed many of its ways but still keeps the core of its centuries-old religious rituals intact.

Historians say the sect was founded in Palestine in the first two centuries after Christ's death but members had to flee to Yemen and from there emigrated to Mesopotamia, the land between Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
SECT TRACES ROOTS TO JOHN THE BAPTIST

In time they developed an elaborate ritual, particularly for baptism. They trace their roots to John the Baptist, whom they revere. A picture of John baptising Jesus adorns the entrance to their temple in Baghdad.
One of their holy books is a form of treatise on cosmology. Another describes the activities of John. Another is a collection of magical and astrological texts.
Abidrabbah and Jabbar were reading a passage describing baptism and purification rituals.
"We believe in God, His angels and Adam. We have our own religion. We are neither Moslems nor Christians," said an old Sabaean. In Iraq they are officially recognised as a separate religion.
Their supreme priest, Sheikh Abdulla Najim al-Zahroon, says only 60,000 of his 100,000-member sect remain in Iraq. The rest have emigrated to the West. Some 15,000 still live in southern Iran.
The Sabaeans used to live among Shi'ite Moslems in the marshes of southern Iraq, where they earned a reputation as the best canoe-makers and the area's most talented carpenters.

But the majority left for Baghdad in the 1950s. The migration from a land of flowing streams and rivers to city life in Baghdad, where the Sabaeans have become Iraq's best silver and goldsmiths, forced Zahroon to introduce reforms.
"Yardana, or flowing water, is of extreme significance in the Sabaean life. It is the basis of all our religious work and rituals," he said.
Yardana could easily be found in the marshes but is not readily available in a city like Baghdad.

Prayer times were reduced from five to three a day and baptism, instead of requiring immersion in a running river or stream after menstruation or sexual intercourse, can now be performed at least once a year in a pool fed by tap water.
The Murda, the place of worship which was traditionally a hut of mud and reeds, has now turned into a fabulous temple on the banks of the Tigris river in Baghdad.
SABAEANS FOLLOW STRICT FOOD LAWS
Eating habits have not changed much over the centuries.
Pig meat is forbidden. Slaughtering sheep or goats and the killing of the female of any animal species is a sin.
Killing of duck, chicken and fish is allowed. But after any killing a Sabaean must still ask forgiveness, preferably through baptism by a priest in the pond.
Priests still have to eat alone or with another of the same rank. Zahroon, the only Reisha Dauma or Head of Nation, always has his meals alone. Tea, coffee and canned food are taboo.
A person willing to become a priest must be of pure lineage, with no physical defects, and pass through at least four lower ranks before attaining the title.
Maxeem Baseem, 21, is a novice. He said he still had to attain the status of Shmolia (student), Talmida (apostle) and Kanza Raba (great treasurer) before Zahroon could ordain him a priest.
